text:
Recent work supports separate encoders for persistent preferences and recent intent, with learned fusion. TLSTSRec (online 2024) combines temporal information with adaptive long/short-term fusion; hierarchical preference modeling (2025) uses dynamic routing to extract multiple long-term interests, then selects those relevant to recent self-attention features and fuses them using time encoding. These approaches suggest conditioning historical retrieval on current intent rather than pooling all older interactions equally. [TLSTSRec](https://doi.org/10.3233/IDA-240051), [hierarchical modeling](https://journal.hep.com.cn/fcs/EN/10.1007/s11704-025-41181-y).

Newer architectures extend this separation across temporal scales. GRELA (2025) introduces gating intended to distinguish local interest from lasting preference shifts. DSRec (September 2026 preprint) pairs a full-sequence Mamba branch with a short-term, time-modulated SSM and residual cross-fusion. TriSSR (2026) motivates separate experts for stable, periodic, and abrupt interest signals, combined through adaptive fusion. These are architectural precedents, not evidence of gains under the pinned RecHarness evaluation. [GRELA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13315), [DSRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.21548), [TriSSR](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0925231226009707).

Practical inference for this task: retain SASRec as a causal backbone, add a recent-window intent branch and an attention-pooled historical branch, then learn a gate from their agreement, history length, and observed time gaps. Compare against fixed mixtures and each branch alone to establish whether adaptive fusion helps. Use timestamps only where available; no demographic, review, or simulator-trait inputs are required for this proposed variant.
